title: What is Directed Studies?
text:
Directed Studies (DS) is a selective, year-long program for first-year students at Yale College. It is an interdisciplinary introduction to influential texts in the Western and Near Eastern traditions, from the ancient Mediterranean to the twentieth century.
The program consists of three integrated, full-year courses taken together:

Literature
Philosophy
Historical and Political Thought

Each course meets weekly for one lecture and two small seminars led by Yale faculty. Roughly ten percent of each first-year class is admitted. Students read heavily and write analytic essays throughout the year, and the essays in this section come from that work.
The fall term covers antiquity through the Middle Ages; the spring term runs from the Renaissance to the twentieth century.
Learn more on the Directed Studies website.

title: Making Decisions Beyond the Chess Board
text:
TEDxColegio Nueva Granada, Bogotá, March 2025.
Every decision framework breaks down under complexity: consequences are unpredictable, intentions are self-serving, and rules are rigid. Drawing on chess, this talk argues that learning to navigate uncertainty is what actually decides outcomes.

title: About Me
text:
I’m Camilo Salgar Duarte, a student at Yale College pursuing a double major in Applied Mathematics and Philosophy (Class of 2029). I grew up in Bogotá, Colombia.
My work sits where mathematical modeling meets philosophy. I’m drawn to questions in AI ethics, existential philosophy, and modernist literature, and to what happens when the tools we build start changing how we understand ourselves. I began at Yale in Directed Studies, and in summer 2026 I studied Mathematical Modelling and the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence at the University of Oxford’s Exeter College Summer Programme.
Outside the classroom, I grade for Yale’s Linear Algebra course, serve as Vice-President of Club Colombia at Yale, and sit on the board of the Yale College Chess Club. I’ve worked on FX and commodity hedging tools at Gestión de Riesgo and studied reinforcement learning at Quantil. I also play competitive chess and follow Independiente Santa Fe.

title: Asymmetric Complexity and the Limits of Engine Evaluation
text:
Exeter College Summer Programme, University of Oxford. Mathematical Modelling, Prof. Tom Crawford. August 2026.
Chess engines report who is better under perfect play, but humans aren’t perfect players. This project models how engine evaluation E and asymmetric complexity C (how much harder a position is for one side than the other) evolve together.
A linear model,

\begin{pmatrix}\dot E\\ \dot C\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha & \beta\\ 0 & \delta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}E\\ C\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha,\beta>0,\ \delta<0,

has a saddle at the origin whose separatrix marks off regions where the engine favors one side but complexity carries the game to the other side’s win. A non-linear extension bounds evaluation and complexity, adds finite win states, and shows a saddle-node bifurcation as advantage begins to generate complexity. The result motivates a more human evaluation metric for broadcasting and chess education.
Methods: linear and non-linear ODEs, phase-plane analysis, bifurcation analysis, Python (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib).

title: AI Should Not Be Called Human-Like: An Approach From Conceptual Engineering
text:
Exeter College Summer Programme, University of Oxford. Ethics of AI, Prof. Christoph Kelp and Prof. Mona Simion. August 2026.
Debates about AI existential risk usually focus on human disempowerment. This paper proposes another kind of existential risk, the self-understanding problem: AI may change what it means to be human.
Using conceptual engineering, it argues two things. First, claims that AI has human-like features (consciousness, cognition, agency) cannot be justified by theories built through anthropocentric abstraction, since those theories can’t non-circularly ground the human standard they rely on. Second, likeness claims made by trusted experts can transfer understanding in both directions, so observations of AI begin to reshape our concept of the human. The paper recommends discussing AI’s features on their own terms and answers two objections.
